claim: An increased perception of pain is generally associated with increased cortical activity in brain regions involved in sensory, emotional, cognitive, and affective aspects of pain.
source: An increased perception of pain is generally associated with increased cortical activity; this has been demonstrated in a number of brain regions and processes involved in sensory, emotional, cognitive, and affective aspects of pain (Coghill and Eisenach, 2003; Tracey and Mantyh, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Coghill and Eisenach, 2003; Tracey and Mantyh, 2007).

claim: Brain regions are required to exchange information to integrate and assess different aspects of pain to compute an appropriate decision and subsequent action.
source: Given the threatening nature of pain, the information processed from these different aspects has to be integrated and assessed to compute an appropriate decision and subsequent action (Liang et al., 2013; Misra and Coombes, 2015; Wiech and Tracey, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Liang et al., 2013; Misra and Coombes, 2015; Wiech and Tracey, 2013).

claim: When pain is worsened by emotional or attentional shifts, this entails increased functional connectivity between relevant cortical and subcortical regions.
source: when pain is worsened by emotional or attentional shifts, this has been shown to entail increased functional connectivity between relevant cortical and subcortical regions (Sprenger et al., 2015; Villemure and Bushnell, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Sprenger et al., 2015; Villemure and Bushnell, 2009).

claim: Less is known about regional brain connectivity changes during decreased pain experiences.
source: Less is known, however, about regional brain connectivity changes during decreased pain experiences, despite some early efforts (Ploner et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Ploner et al., 2011) and represents a knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: Several studies have investigated the influence of pain on ICA-based functional networks.
source: Several studies have investigated the influence of pain on Independent Component Analysis (ICA)-based functional networks (Kucyi et al., 2013; Seminowicz and Davis, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kucyi et al., 2013; Seminowicz and Davis, 2007).

claim: Villemure and Bushnell, 2009 and Ploner et al., 2011 observed an increase of connectivity for conditions that increased the intensity of pain.
source: Villemure and Bushnell, 2009 and Ploner et al., 2011, for example, investigated the influence of different levels of emotion and attention, respectively, on cortical connectivity between brain regions involved in pain and emotional processing. Both studies observed an increase of connectivity for the conditions that increased the intensity of pain.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Villemure and Bushnell, 2009; Ploner et al., 2011).

claim: A change in pre-stimulus cortical connectivity patterns from the anterior insula to the PAG determined whether a subsequent nociceptive stimulus was perceived as painful or not.
source: A different study found that a change in pre-stimulus cortical connectivity patterns from the anterior insula to the periaqueductal grey (PAG), which is part of the descending pain modulatory system (Sprenger et al., 2018), determined whether a subsequent nociceptive stimulus was perceived as painful or not (Ploner et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Ploner et al., 2010; Sprenger et al., 2018).

claim: The PAG is part of the descending pain modulatory system.
source: A different study found that a change in pre-stimulus cortical connectivity patterns from the anterior insula to the periaqueductal grey (PAG), which is part of the descending pain modulatory system (Sprenger et al., 2018), determined whether a subsequent nociceptive stimulus was perceived as painful or not (Ploner et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Sprenger et al., 2018).

claim: Increased activity or functional connectivity between the PAG and the rACC is associated with decreased pain intensity perception in conditions such as placebo and shift of attention.
source: Supporting that observation, other investigations have similarly reported an increased activity or functional connectivity between the PAG and the rostral anterior cingulate cortex (rACC) for conditions associated with decreased pain intensity perception (e.g. placebo, shift of attention) (Bantick et al., 2002; Eippert et al., 2009; Sprenger et al., 2012; Tracey et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bantick et al., 2002; Eippert et al., 2009; Sprenger et al., 2012; Tracey et al., 2002).

claim: Functional connections are likely supported by the structural integrity of white matter tracts between brain regions, as measured using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI).
source: These functional connections are likely supported by the structural integrity of white matter tracts between brain regions, as measured using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between structural and functional connectivity.

claim: The structural integrity of components of the descending pain modulatory system were significantly correlated to the effectiveness in alleviating pain through transcranial direct current stimulation.
source: Indeed, a study has confirmed that the structural integrity of components of the descending pain modulatory system were significantly correlated to the effectiveness in alleviating pain through transcranial direct current stimulation (Lin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Lin et al., 2017).

claim: The precise nature of connectivity changes within the whole brain, especially during decreased pain, is still unclear.
source: However, the precise nature of connectivity changes within the whole brain, especially during decreased pain, is still unclear.
evidence: The claim represents a knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: Ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) facilitates single-trial analysis.
source: Using ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) that facilitates single-trial analysis, we examined the whole-brain functional connections that contribute to the attenuation of pain.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the capabilities of ultra-high-field fMRI.

claim: The study used three different cognitive interventions: non-imaginal distraction by counting backwards, imaginal distraction by imagining a safe place, and reinterpretation of the pain valence (cognitive reappraisal).
source: We used three different cognitive interventions: (a) a non-imaginal distraction by counting backwards in steps of seven; (b) an imaginal distraction by imagining a safe place; and (c) reinterpretation of the pain valence (cognitive reappraisal).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Healthy participants were asked to utilise cognitive strategies in order to attenuate the experience of pain during 40 s of cold stimulation.
source: Healthy participants were asked to utilise cognitive strategies in order to attenuate the experience of pain during 40 s of cold stimulation.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: A whole-brain parcellation approach was used to assess every cortical connection that contributes to pain relief.
source: We pursued a whole-brain parcellation approach (Glasser et al., 2016) in order to assess every cortical connection that contributes to pain relief.
evidence: The claim describes the analytical approach of the study, with a citation to the parcellation method (Glasser et al., 2016).

claim: All three interventions resulted in a significant reduction in the ratings of perceived pain compared to the unmodulated pain condition.
source: Behavioural data revealed a significant reduction in the ratings of perceived pain for all three interventions compared to the unmodulated pain condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from the study.

claim: For the counting condition, pain attenuation was 21 (±2.55 SE) for pain intensity and 19 (±2.87 SE) for pain unpleasantness (p<0.05).
source: For example, for the counting condition we observed a pain attenuation of 21 (±2.55 SE) for pain intensity and of 19 (±2.87 SE) for pain unpleasantness (p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data from the study.

claim: Pain during the cognitive task trials was rated as less painful and had a stronger global brain connectivity compared to trials where there was no cognitive modulation.
source: Globally, we found increased connectivity during pain attenuation: pain during the cognitive task trials was rated as less painful and had a stronger global brain connectivity compared to trials where there was no cognitive modulation (i.e. the unmodulated pain condition).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing the relationship between pain ratings and connectivity.

claim: Trials at higher levels of pain are coupled with low connectivity, and trials at lower levels of pain are coupled with high connectivity.
source: Therefore, trials at higher levels of pain are coupled with low connectivity, and trials at lower levels of pain are coupled with high connectivity.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the data showing the relationship between pain levels and connectivity.

claim: The cortex was subdivided into 180 regions per hemisphere, plus 11 subcortical regions for the whole-brain approach.
source: We pursued a whole-brain approach by subdividing the cortex into 180 regions per hemisphere, plus 11 subcortical regions (Glasser et al., 2016), and related cortical connectivity to pain ratings at a single trial level.
evidence: The claim describes the analytical approach of the study, with a citation to the parcellation method (Glasser et al., 2016).

claim: The single-trial analysis approach was facilitated by increased signal-to-noise as a result of ultra-high field imaging.
source: This approach was facilitated by the increased signal-to-noise as a result of ultra-high field imaging, as well as by a more robust assessment of single-trial data from longer lasting painful stimulation and an extended task application.
evidence: The claim is based on the methodological advantages of ultra-high field imaging.

claim: Positive relationships (red) in the confusion matrices show connectivities that were increased in particularly effective pain attenuation trials (performance encoding).
source: In the present study, positive relationships (red) show connectivities that were increased in particularly effective pain attenuation trials (performance encoding).
evidence: The claim describes the interpretation of the data visualization in the study.

claim: Across all tasks, increased connectivity of task-processing brain regions is related to particularly effective attempts to attenuate pain.
source: Across all tasks, we confirmed our first hypothesis by showing that increased connectivity of task-processing brain regions (see Schulz et al., 2019) is related to particularly effective attempts to attenuate pain.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and references a prior publication (Schulz et al., 2019).

claim: Negative relationships (blue) represent cortical connections that are disrupted in effective pain attenuation trials.
source: Negative relationships (blue) represent cortical connections that are disrupted in effective pain attenuation trials.
evidence: The claim describes the interpretation of the data visualization in the study.

claim: Regions that belong to brain regions long associated with pain processing (insular and cingulate cortices) predominantly showed increased connectivity during effective pain attenuation trials.
source: However, we found that these regions predominantly showed increased connectivity during effective pain attenuation trials.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing connectivity patterns in pain-related regions.

claim: An association was observed between low pain and high connectivity for regions that belong to brain regions long associated with pain processing, the insular and cingulate cortices.
source: Of note, we observed an association between low pain and high connectivity for regions that belong to brain regions long associated with pain processing, the insular and cingulate cortices.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing the relationship between pain levels and connectivity in specific brain regions.

claim: For the counting condition, 171 connections were significantly increased or decreased out of 68635 potential functional connections.
source: Out of 68635 potential functional connections, we found 171 connections were significantly increased or decreased during the counting condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from the study.

claim: During the counting condition, there was a general increase of cortical connectivity with the exception of decreased connections involving the right temporo-parieto-occipital junction.
source: we found a general increase of cortical connectivity with the exception of decreased connections involving the right temporo-parieto-occipital junction (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and references Figure 1A.

claim: The most connected area during the counting condition is the right middle insula (R_MI).
source: The most connected area is the right middle insula (R_MI, Figure 1C; for the nomenclature of these regions see Glasser et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and references Figure 1C and the Glasser parcellation (Glasser et al., 2016).

claim: The right middle insula was decreased in activity during pain attenuation.
source: Our earlier publication reported that the right middle insula was decreased in activity during pain attenuation (see Schulz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior publication (Schulz et al., 2019).

claim: The right middle insula might suppress activity in the posterior cingulate cortex (L_23 c, R_23 c).
source: We suggest it might suppress activity in the posterior cingulate cortex (L_23 c, R_23 c).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the connectivity patterns observed.

claim: There are intra-hemispheric connectivity increases between subdivisions of the insular cortices but no increases between subdivisions of the right insula itself during the counting condition.
source: There are intra-hemispheric connectivity increases between subdivisions of the insular cortices but, interestingly, no increases between subdivisions of the right insula itself.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing connectivity patterns.

claim: There was no significant change in connectivity to subcortical areas during the counting condition.
source: There was no significant change in connectivity to subcortical areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing no significant subcortical connectivity changes.

claim: An increased functional connectivity with pain attenuation was confirmed for the counting condition in the network of areas related to the 'NPS' (p<0.05, uncorrected).
source: We confirmed an increased functional connectivity with pain attenuation for the counting condition in the network of areas related to the "NPS" (p<0.05, uncorrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study.

claim: Measures of structural connectivity (DTI fibre tracking) did not explain interindividual differences in modulating task-related functional connections in the counting condition.
source: Interestingly, measures of structural connectivity (DTI fibre tracking) did not explain interindividual differences in modulating task-related functional connections in the counting condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing no relationship between structural and functional connectivity for this condition.

claim: For the safe place condition, 210 functional connections were significantly increased or decreased.
source: We found 210 functional connections that were significantly increased or decreased during the imagining condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from the study.

claim: There was an increase of connectivity across all cortical regions during the safe place condition when compared to the unmodulated pain condition.
source: We found an increase of connectivity across all cortical regions when compared to the unmodulated pain condition (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and references Figure 2A.

claim: There was no negative relationship between single-trial connectivity and pain intensity during the safe place condition.
source: There was no negative relationship between single-trial connectivity and pain intensity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing no negative correlations.

claim: For the safe place condition, a main hub for functional connectivity is the right insular cortex.
source: For this safe condition, we again found that a main hub for functional connectivity is the right insular cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing connectivity patterns.

claim: There was no significant connectivity change to subcortical areas during the safe place condition.
source: There was no significant connectivity change to subcortical areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing no significant subcortical connectivity changes.

claim: An increased functional connectivity with pain attenuation was confirmed for the 'safe place' condition in the network of areas related to the 'NPS' (p<0.001, uncorrected).
source: We confirmed an increased functional connectivity with pain attenuation for the 'safe place' condition in the network of areas related to the "NPS" (p<0.001, uncorrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study.

claim: For the 'safe place' condition only, white matter structural connectivity as measured using DTI mediates the strength of the functional connectivity.
source: For this 'safe place' condition only, we found that white matter structural connectivity, as measured using DTI, mediates the strength of the functional connectivity (Source data 4_DTI).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing a relationship between structural and functional connectivity for this condition.

claim: For the safe place condition, strong structural connectivities are related to a better ability to modulate the functional connectivity in order to attenuate pain.
source: Strong structural connectivities are related to a better ability to modulate the functional connectivity in order to attenuate pain.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing the relationship between structural connectivity and pain attenuation ability.

claim: For the safe place condition, functional connections between frontal regions (IFSp and Brodmann area 8C) and the secondary somatosensory cortex (SII) are supported by the strength of fibre connections.
source: This applies especially to connections between frontal regions (IFSp and Brodmann area 8C) and the secondary somatosensory cortex (SII).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing the relationship between structural and functional connectivity.

claim: For the safe place condition, functional connections that are supported by the strength of fibre connections projected to memory-related areas (presubiculum of the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex).
source: Further functional connections that are supported by the strength of fibre connections, projected to memory-related areas (presubiculum of the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing the relationship between structural and functional connectivity.

claim: During cognitive reappraisal, a pain attenuation-related increase of functional connectivity was found compared to the unmodulated pain condition across the entire cortex.
source: While executing cognitive reappraisal, we found a pain attenuation-related increase of functional connectivity compared to the unmodulated pain condition across the entire cortex (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and references Figure 3A.

claim: Decreased functional connectivity was not observed during cognitive reappraisal.
source: Decreased functional connectivity was not observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing no negative connectivity changes.

claim: During cognitive reappraisal, connections that included frontal premotor and insular sub-regions contributed to a decrease of pain.
source: Connections that included frontal premotor and insular sub-regions contributed to a decrease of pain (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and references Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: During cognitive reappraisal, the main hub of connectivity was located in the medial parieto-occipital cortex.
source: However, the main hub of connectivity was located in the medial parieto-occipital cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing connectivity patterns.

claim: The structural characteristics between cortical regions did not contribute to an enhanced functional connectivity for reappraisal.
source: The structural characteristics between cortical regions did not contribute to an enhanced functional connectivity for reappraisal.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing no relationship between structural and functional connectivity for this condition.

claim: There was no significant connectivity change to subcortical areas during cognitive reappraisal.
source: Again, there was no significant connectivity change to subcortical areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing no significant subcortical connectivity changes.

claim: An increased functional connectivity with pain attenuation was confirmed for the reappraisal condition in the network of areas related to the 'NPS' (p<0.005, uncorrected).
source: We confirmed an increased functional connectivity with pain attenuation for the reappraisal condition in the network of areas related to the "NPS" (p<0.005, uncorrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study.

claim: No connectivity changes related to pain modulation were present in all three conditions.
source: We did not find any connectivity changes related to pain modulation that were present in all three conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing no common connectivity changes across all conditions.

claim: For the counting condition, 63 regions had a stronger effect compared to the other two conditions.
source: For the counting condition, we found 63 regions that had a stronger effect compared to the other two conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study comparing conditions.

claim: For the safe place condition, 7 regions were more strongly connected compared to the other conditions.
source: Similarly, 7 regions for 'safe place' and 11 regions for reappraisal were more strongly connected compared to the other conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study comparing conditions.

claim: For the reappraisal condition, 11 regions were more strongly connected compared to the other conditions.
source: Similarly, 7 regions for 'safe place' and 11 regions for reappraisal were more strongly connected compared to the other conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study comparing conditions.

claim: The participants were assumed to execute the tasks with considerable motivation as their effort would be rewarded with decreased pain intensity and pain unpleasantness.
source: The participants were assumed to execute the tasks with considerable motivation as their effort would be rewarded with decreased pain intensity and pain unpleasantness (Huskey et al., 2018; Pochon et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is an assumption based on citations to prior research on motivation (Huskey et al., 2018; Pochon et al., 2002).

claim: The functional connections identified are interpreted in light of a recently reported study that determined the changes in regional BOLD activity during successful single attempts to attenuate pain.
source: The functional connections identified here are interpreted in light of our recently reported study that determined the changes in regional BOLD activity during successful single attempts to attenuate pain – drawn from the same data set used for this connectivity analysis (Schulz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim references a prior publication (Schulz et al., 2019) that used the same dataset.

claim: Non-imaginal reinterpretation (reappraisal) and the imaginal strategy (safe place) predominantly involved modulation of the anterior insula.
source: In that study, non-imaginal reinterpretation (reappraisal) and the imaginal strategy (safe place) predominantly involved modulation of the anterior insula, the non-imaginal distraction task (counting backwards) predominantly modulated the central operculum, whereas tasks that involved distraction from pain (counting, safe place) modulated posterior cingulate cortex activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior publication (Schulz et al., 2019).

claim: The non-imaginal distraction task (counting backwards) predominantly modulated the central operculum.
source: In that study, non-imaginal reinterpretation (reappraisal) and the imaginal strategy (safe place) predominantly involved modulation of the anterior insula, the non-imaginal distraction task (counting backwards) predominantly modulated the central operculum, whereas tasks that involved distraction from pain (counting, safe place) modulated posterior cingulate cortex activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior publication (Schulz et al., 2019).

claim: Tasks that involved distraction from pain (counting, safe place) modulated posterior cingulate cortex activity.
source: In that study, non-imaginal reinterpretation (reappraisal) and the imaginal strategy (safe place) predominantly involved modulation of the anterior insula, the non-imaginal distraction task (counting backwards) predominantly modulated the central operculum, whereas tasks that involved distraction from pain (counting, safe place) modulated posterior cingulate cortex activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior publication (Schulz et al., 2019).

claim: It is still not completely clear how cognitive tasks are executed through functional interactions between brain regions to modulate painful experiences.
source: It is still not completely clear how cognitive tasks are executed through functional interactions between brain regions to modulate painful experiences.
evidence: The claim represents a knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: There is no seed-based whole-brain investigation on how the experience of pain fluctuates across trials driven by the variable strength of cortical connections.
source: Additionally, there is no seed-based whole-brain investigation on how the experience of pain fluctuates across trials driven by the variable strength of cortical connections.
evidence: The claim represents a knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: For each of the regions from the Glasser parcellation, a subject-wise principal component analysis (PCA) was computed to relate the time-course to other brain regions.
source: It should be noted that for each of the regions from the Glasser parcellation, we computed a subject-wise principal component analysis (PCA) to relate the time-course to other brain regions.
evidence: The claim describes the analytical approach of the study.

claim: Across all cognitive interventions, results revealed a global increase of connectivity throughout the cerebral cortex for all three interventions.
source: Across all cognitive interventions, our results revealed a global increase of connectivity throughout the cerebral cortex for all three interventions: higher functional connectivity was related to particularly effective single attempts to attenuate pain.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing connectivity patterns across conditions.

claim: Higher functional connectivity was related to particularly effective single attempts to attenuate pain across all cognitive interventions.
source: Across all cognitive interventions, our results revealed a global increase of connectivity throughout the cerebral cortex for all three interventions: higher functional connectivity was related to particularly effective single attempts to attenuate pain.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing the relationship between connectivity and pain attenuation.

claim: The unmodulated pain trials exhibited a lower functional connectivity compared to pain trials during cognitive tasks.
source: Therefore, the unmodulated pain trials - which were experienced as considerably more painful - exhibited a lower functional connectivity compared to pain trials during cognitive tasks.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study comparing connectivity between conditions.

claim: Increased connectivity in task-related regions is necessary to effectively execute the respective cognitive tasks.
source: First, increased connectivity in task-related regions is necessary to effectively execute the respective cognitive tasks.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the data showing the relationship between connectivity and task performance.

claim: The increased connectivity is required to actively suppress activity in regions known to contribute to pain processing.
source: We suggest that this increased connectivity is required to actively suppress activity in regions known to contribute to pain processing, as previously reported for these tasks (Schulz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the connectivity patterns and a citation to a prior publication (Schulz et al., 2019).

claim: There are GABAergic neurons in subregions of the insular cortex.
source: We do not know the nature of such regional suppression; however, there are GABAergic neurons in subregions of the insular cortex (Watson, 2016; Thiaucourt et al., 2018), and these might possibly contribute.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Watson, 2016; Thiaucourt et al., 2018).

claim: GABAergic neurons in subregions of the insular cortex might possibly contribute to regional suppression during pain attenuation.
source: We do not know the nature of such regional suppression; however, there are GABAergic neurons in subregions of the insular cortex (Watson, 2016; Thiaucourt et al., 2018), and these might possibly contribute.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from known neurobiology and citations to prior research (Watson, 2016; Thiaucourt et al., 2018).

claim: Each cognitive intervention has its own pattern of intra-cortical connectivity.
source: Besides the general observation of increased connectivity, which is linked to higher task performance and lower pain, each cognitive intervention has its own pattern of intra-cortical connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing different connectivity patterns for each condition.

claim: The execution of the counting task is suggested to require visual support by imagining the numbers in space.
source: The execution of the counting task is suggested to require visual support by imagining the numbers in space (Amalric and Dehaene, 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on a citation to prior research (Amalric and Dehaene, 2016).

claim: Visual areas in the left occipito-temporal cortex connect to and suppress right parietal opercular areas during the counting task.
source: Visual areas in the left occipito-temporal cortex connect to and suppress right parietal opercular areas.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the connectivity patterns observed in the data.

claim: The functional connectivities between left parietal areas (high BOLD activity) and right insular sub-regions (low BOLD activity) support a likely suppression effect on these insular regions during the counting task.
source: Although our analyses do not allow for any assumptions on directionality, the functional connectivities between left parietal areas (high BOLD activity) and right insular sub-regions (low BOLD activity) support a likely suppression effect on these insular regions (Schulz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the connectivity patterns and BOLD activity data, with a citation to a prior publication (Schulz et al., 2019).

claim: The highly connected superior temporal region is suggested to support the retrieval of mathematical knowledge during the counting task.
source: The highly connected superior temporal region is suggested to support the retrieval of mathematical knowledge (Polspoel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on a citation to prior research (Polspoel et al., 2017).

claim: Disrupted connectivities during the counting task were observed for the right temporo-parieto-occipital junction (TPJ) to the right posterior insula, as well as to temporo-occipital areas.
source: Disrupted connectivities during the counting task were observed for the right temporo-parieto-occipital junction (TPJ) to the right posterior insula, as well as to temporo-occipital areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study showing connectivity patterns.

claim: The TPJ is involved in attentional processing.
source: Given the involvement of the TPJ in attentional processing (Kucyi et al., 2012; Mars et al., 2012), elevated focus on the task may have decreased nociceptive transmission to the posterior insula during task execution but increased the transmission for unmodulated pain trials (Schulz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kucyi et al., 2012; Mars et al., 2012).

claim: Elevated focus on the counting task may have decreased nociceptive transmission to the posterior insula during task execution but increased the transmission for unmodulated pain trials.
source: Given the involvement of the TPJ in attentional processing (Kucyi et al., 2012; Mars et al., 2012), elevated focus on the task may have decreased nociceptive transmission to the posterior insula during task execution but increased the transmission for unmodulated pain trials (Schulz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the connectivity patterns and citations to prior research (Kucyi et al., 2012; Mars et al., 2012; Schulz et al., 2019).

claim: The bilateral parietal cortex (area five right, area seven left) is functionally connected without a concomitant rise of regional BOLD activity during the safe place condition.
source: Notably, the bilateral parietal cortex (area five right, area seven left) is functionally connected without a concomitant rise of regional BOLD activity (Schulz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and a citation to a prior publication (Schulz et al., 2019).

claim: Regional activity changes or connectivity changes between regions play complementary roles when modulating painful experiences.
source: This finding highlights the complementary roles that both regional activity changes or connectivity changes between regions play when modulating painful experiences: active exchange of information with potentially low-scale modulations of cortical activity that are not causing large and measurable metabolic effects.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the data showing connectivity without BOLD activity changes.

claim: The strong connectivity pattern between left parietal and right insular sub-regions suggests an active suppression of these insular regions initiated by the parietal cortex during the safe place condition.
source: Possibly, the strong connectivity pattern between left parietal and right insular sub-regions suggests an active suppression of these insular regions initiated by the parietal cortex, as reflected by increased functional connectivity between these regions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the connectivity patterns observed.

claim: Area 55b has been shown to be active during listening to stories in the language task of the Human Connectome Project dataset.
source: area 55b has been shown to be active during listening to stories in the language task of the Human Connectome Project dataset (Glasser et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Glasser et al., 2016).

claim: The increased connectivity in area 55b may be related to the narrative aspects of the imaginary task during the safe place condition.
source: Therefore, the increased connectivity in area 55b may be related to the narrative aspects of the imaginary task, in which the participants may recall being actively involved in an event of pleasure and happiness.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the connectivity patterns and the nature of the task.

claim: The premotor and motor areas in the precentral gyrus may reflect the motor aspect of the imagination task during the safe place condition.
source: The premotor and motor areas in the precentral gyrus in particular may reflect the motor aspect of the imagination task (Szameitat et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the connectivity patterns and citations to prior research (Szameitat et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2015).

claim: Premotor and motor areas are connected to orbitofrontal regions that have been highlighted as important in mediating predictive cues about pain in conditioning and placebo studies.
source: They are connected to orbitofrontal regions that have been highlighted as important in mediating predictive cues about pain in conditioning and placebo studies (with involvement of the descending pain modulatory inhibitory network; Atlas et al., 2010; Bingel et al., 2007; Eippert et al., 2009) as well as studies highlighting the role of the orbitofrontal cortex in threat valuation of pain during attentional guiding in clinical studies (Scharmüller et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Atlas et al., 2010; Bingel et al., 2007; Eippert et al., 2009; Scharmüller et al., 2014).

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex plays a role in threat valuation of pain during attentional guiding in clinical studies.
